entries.text: The authors test intracortical decoding from dorsal precentral ‘hand knob’ arrays as a lower-bound proof of concept for speech BCIs, using overt spoken words rather than attempted speech.
entries.condition: Two BrainGate2 participants able to speak; each had two chronic 96-electrode Utah arrays in left dorsal motor cortex.
entries.quote: Neural and audio data were recorded while two BrainGate2 pilot clinical trial participants, each with two chronically-implanted 96-electrode arrays, spoke 420 different words that broadly sampled English phonemes.

entries.text: The authors argue that arrays in ventral speech cortex are a promising next direction because decoding from arrays in a nontraditional dorsal area was feasible.
entries.condition: Proposed future work; this study recorded only dorsal precentral gyrus and did not test ventral arrays.
entries.quote: Future efforts will benefit from access to ventral speech cortex as well as higher electrode counts that record from a larger neural population.

entries.text: The Many Words Task recorded two participants speaking a 420-word set broadly sampling English phonemes.
entries.condition: T5 and T11; visually prompted overt speech; 39 phoneme classes used for classification.

entries.text: Phoneme-specific analyses used 39 classes: classes needed at least 30 T5 repetitions, one T11 class with 26 repetitions was retained, and two sparse pairs were merged (/ɔ/ with /ʌ/; /ɚ/ with /ɝ/).
entries.condition: T5/T11 utterances from the 420-word task; the two mergers were made to increase counts for low-frequency classes.

entries.text: T5 completed three repetitions of each word (12 blocks); T11 completed 11 blocks for two to three repetitions per word; the corpus was divided across four blocks.
entries.value: T5: 3 repetitions/12 blocks; T11: 11 blocks/2–3 repetitions; 4 corpus blocks
entries.condition: 420 visually prompted words; one session per participant’s reported Many Words Task dataset.

entries.text: Each participant had two 96-electrode arrays in left dorsal motor cortex; arrays were implanted 29 months before T5’s session and 3 months before T11’s.
entries.condition: Utah arrays in the ‘hand knob’ area; T5 and T11 respectively.

entries.text: Neural signals were digitized at 30 kHz/16 bits after 0.3–7,500 Hz analog filtering; HLFP was extracted with a causal 125–5,000 Hz filter and TC spikes used a −3.5×RMS voltage threshold without spike sorting.
entries.condition: NeuroPort acquisition; Utah arrays; features for the two participants’ overt-speech sessions.

entries.text: One noisy trial per participant was removed; HLFP was clipped at 100×electrode median, smoothed over 20 ms at 1 ms spacing, and visual quality screening retained 158 T5 and 179 T11 electrodes.
entries.unit: trial/participant; median multiplier; ms; ms; electrodes
entries.condition: Preprocessing before neural analyses; T5 and T11 separately.

entries.text: The exact utterance counts were 3,840 for T5 and 3,467 for T11; the distributions differed because of different block counts and occasional misspeaking or homophones.
entries.condition: Many Words Task; same word prompt set, 420 words, but participant-specific realized utterances.

entries.text: Logistic regression usually used 500 ms centered on phoneme onset, non-overlapping 50 ms bins, fold-wise z-scoring, and PCA retaining 75% variance; normalization/PCA statistics were fit on training folds only.
entries.condition: Phoneme classification; unless otherwise stated; onset labels came from audio.
entries.quote: Except where otherwise mentioned, we extracted a 500 millisecond window of neural activity centered around the onset of each phoneme.

entries.text: The linear decoder reached 29.3% accuracy (reported as 29.29% in Results) on T5’s 39-phoneme classification task; the abstract reports 6% chance.
entries.condition: Offline logistic regression on T5 overt prompted utterances; 420-word task, 39 classes; Fig. 3A uses leave-one-out CV; audio-onset-centered windows. No language model or online feedback.

entries.text: Across 39 classes, TC-spike accuracy was 14.8% for T5 and 7.9% for T11; HLFP accuracy was 29.29% and 11.22%, respectively.
entries.condition: Offline logistic regression; overt prompted words; approximately 14 total minutes across the data; audio-labeled phoneme windows, generally 500 ms; T5/T11 each evaluated within participant by CV.
entries.quote: Our first major observation was that although TC-spikes contained substantial information about phoneme identity (14.8% accuracy for T5, 7.9% accuracy for T11, p < 0.002 compared to chance), classification was much more accurate when decoding high-frequency local field potential power (HLFP, 125-5000 Hz): 29.29% and 11.22% for T5 and T11 respectively (Fig. 3A,F).

entries.text: The paper reports 6% chance for 39-class classification but does not state how that chance baseline was calculated (for example, uniform guessing versus class-prior baseline).
entries.condition: Abstract classification comparison; 39 phoneme labels.
entries.quote: A linear decoder achieved up to 29.3% classification accuracy (chance = 6%) across 39 phonemes, while a recurrent neural network classifier achieved 33.9% accuracy.

entries.text: Parameter sweeps showed no saturation as training data or electrode count increased, and finer time bins improved accuracy; this supports collecting more data and recording sites.
entries.condition: T5 and T11 sweeps; repeated 10-fold CV for sweep plots; improvements are limited by the observed participant/session datasets.

entries.text: At least one phoneme modulated 156/158 T5 electrodes and 179/179 T11 electrodes; at least half of the 39 classes modulated 40/158 and 41/179 electrodes, respectively.
entries.condition: Single-electrode firing-rate changes between a 500 ms delay window and 100 ms around phoneme voice onset; T5/T11 datasets; uncorrected permutation sign tests.

entries.text: Significant firing-rate changes were increases around voice onset in 78% of T5 changes and 86% of T11 changes.
entries.condition: Overt speaking; participant-specific significant firing-rate changes across electrodes and phonemes.

entries.text: In a matched comparison, T5 reached 36.8% across 24 consonant classes and 27.7% across 16 vowel classes; the cited best Mugler ECoG participant scored 36.1% and 23.9%.
entries.condition: T5 offline phoneme classification; matched word subset, trial count matched to Mugler’s best participant, 600 ms audio-onset-centered window; comparator is prior ECoG study.
entries.quote: Decoding vowels and consonants separately as in, the T5 dataset accuracy was 36.8% across 24 consonant classes (vs. 36.1% in Mugler et al.’s best participant) and 27.7% across 16 vowels classes (vs. 23.9%).

entries.text: The matched-comparison word count is inconsistent within the paper: Methods says 256 of Mugler’s 320 words were present; Results says 232 were shared and 80 replaced.
entries.condition: Matched T5–Mugler ECoG comparison; this discrepancy affects the exact vocabulary overlap condition.
entries.quote: Our word set already had 256 of the 320 words of that study; these we included in our ‘matched’ data subset.

entries.text: The RNN used one 512-unit bidirectional GRU layer on 192-channel HLFP snippets of 1,000 ms in 50 bins; its final-bin 39-class prediction was evaluated in 10 folds.
entries.unit: GRU units; channels; ms; bins; classes; folds
entries.condition: T5 RNN analysis used all 192 electrodes; each utterance appeared in the test set once.

entries.text: The abstract reports RNN accuracy of 33.9% for the 39-phoneme task.
entries.condition: T5 RNN; offline overt-speech phoneme classification on the 420-word task; all 192 electrodes; 10-fold utterance-level CV; 1,000 ms/50-bin input, last-bin prediction; no LM or online feedback.
entries.quote: A linear decoder achieved up to 29.3% classification accuracy (chance = 6%) across 39 phonemes, while a recurrent neural network classifier achieved 33.9% accuracy.

entries.text: Results report 33.4% RNN versus 29.6% logistic regression with matched input data; Discussion instead reports 33.9% versus 29.6%.
entries.condition: T5; RNN with data augmentation and logistic regression on identical input and the same 10 CV folds; 39-phoneme task. The RNN value differs between Results and Discussion/Abstract.
entries.quote: However, this resulted in only a modest performance improvement (33.4% accuracy versus 29.6% for a logistic regression with matched input data; Supplementary Figure 3).

entries.text: Using the same electrode exclusions as the linear decoder gave the RNN 32.4%, versus 33.9% with all 192 electrodes.
entries.condition: T5; RNN 39-class task; same input/folds otherwise; comparison is 158 retained electrodes versus all 192 electrodes.

entries.text: RNN training used L2 λ=1e−5, white input noise SD=0.1, per-utterance offset drift SD=0.6, random-walk drift SD=0.02, Adam batches of 128 and 20,000 minibatches; learning rate decayed 0.01 to 0.
entries.unit: regularization; SD; SD; SD; utterances/batch; minibatches; learning rate
entries.condition: T5 RNN training; 10 data folds; augmentation applied during training; no burn-in steps.

entries.text: Neural realignment reduced first-phoneme accuracy from 54.9% with audio-onset alignment to 47.8% across 18 classes, a reported relative decrease of 12.9%.
entries.condition: T5; first phoneme of each word only; 18 classes; 500 ms windows; 20-fold CV; audio-onset versus CIS1 neural-onset alignment.
entries.quote: Decoding each word’s first phoneme from neural data time windows centered on neurally-derived phoneme onsets yielded 47.8% accuracy across 18 classes (Fig. 4E), as compared to 54.9% using windows centered on audio-derived phoneme onsets (Fig. 4D), a relative decrease of 12.9%.

entries.text: Using only the 500 ms before voice onset decoded the first phoneme at 34.8% across 18 classes; the reported significance was p<0.002 with 500 permutations.
entries.unit: % accuracy; classes; CV folds; permutations; p-value
entries.condition: T5; first phoneme of prompted words; pre-voice window avoids audible acoustic contamination and auditory feedback; offline 20-fold CV.
entries.quote: Decoding these pre-voice neural windows for each word’s first phoneme yielded a cross-validated (20 fold) classification performance of 34.8% across 18 classes (Fig. 5F), well above chance performance (p < 0.002; permutation test, 500 permutations).

entries.text: LRR reduced full 39-class accuracy from 29.3% to 25.8% after regression decontamination.
entries.condition: T5; all 39 phonemes; offline cross-validated classification; 500 ms audio-onset-centered windows; LRR predicts each electrode from others using within-block fits.
entries.quote: At the same time, there was only a small reduction in cross-validated accuracy decoding all phonemes (reduction from 29.3% to 25.8%, Fig. 5D), indicating that the procedure was not eliminating much phoneme-specific information.

entries.text: Figure 5E shows 43.5% accuracy after LRR for first-phoneme decoding.
entries.condition: T5; first phoneme of each word; 18 classes; 500 ms window centered on voice onset; figure panel reports the value.

entries.text: In one example block, maximum audio–neural correlation was r=0.953 and median r=−0.002 across 192 electrodes × 240 frequency bins (46,080 comparisons).
entries.condition: T5 audio and electrode PSD during voicing epochs; correlations inspected across frequencies; maximum is an example-block extreme, not aggregate decoding performance.

entries.text: The mean audio–neural correlation reduction after LRR was 0.26.
entries.condition: Pooled across blocks, electrodes, and frequencies for electrodes with original r²>0.1; not a decoding accuracy metric.

entries.text: Offline Brain-to-Speech synthesis achieved mean r=0.523 between true and reconstructed audio, averaged across 40 Mel-frequency-bin correlations.
entries.condition: T5 only; 10-fold CV over Many Words Task data; test-fold words excluded from training; neural pattern matching without a language model or concatenation cost.
entries.quote: Averaging across all the data and all forty bins, the mean correlation was 0.523.

entries.text: Randomly selecting training audio units yielded chance synthesis correlations from 0.019 to 0.038, mean 0.027.
entries.condition: Speech-synthesis chance procedure; 100 random best-match unit selections; T5 held-out data and same spectral metric.

entries.text: The target paper reports Herff et al.’s ECoG synthesis correlations as r=0.574 for the best participant and r=0.246 averaged across six participants.
entries.condition: Prior Herff et al. ECoG speech-synthesis study; best participant versus six-participant mean; comparison metric as reported by the target paper.
entries.quote: Herff and colleagues report an accuracy of r = 0.574 for the best participant in their ECoG study, and r = 0.246 averaged across all six participants.

entries.text: For the nine selected good example words shown in Fig. 6, the mean correlation across 40 Mel bins was 0.696; the paper separately says most synthesis trials were not intelligible.
entries.condition: T5; selected showcase examples, not the full held-out set; Fig. 6 visual panel.

entries.text: The target paper reports 21% accuracy across 38 phonemes for a prior intracortical phoneme-decoding study, below its own best T5 result.
entries.condition: Prior intracortical study cited in Discussion; target paper gives no additional split, participant, or session details in this comparison sentence.

entries.text: The authors claim high-frequency LFP decoding outperformed threshold-crossing spikes in this 39-phoneme task, while explicitly cautioning that this does not mean spike-band power universally carries more information than action potentials.
entries.condition: Observed on these chronic arrays and datasets, where many electrodes lacked isolatable single units or large-amplitude multiunit crossings.

entries.text: The authors identify audio-derived phoneme-onset labels as a possible source of systematic between-phoneme timing bias and introduce CIS1-based neural realignment as a correction.
entries.condition: Realignment was evaluated only for the first phoneme of each word; later phonemes lacked reliable neural timing signals.

entries.text: The authors identify overt-speech microphonic contamination and onset-label bias as confounds that modestly inflate measured decoding; both can be mitigated but neither is fully eliminated.
entries.condition: Acoustic artifact subtraction/LRR and neural onset alignment; the remaining confound contribution is not exactly isolated.
entries.quote: Microphonic contamination and phoneme onset differences modestly increased decoding accuracy, but could be mitigated by acoustic artifact subtraction and using a neural speech onset marker, respectively.

entries.text: The authors describe the results as competitive with prior ECoG classification/synthesis performance, but later warn the comparisons are ballpark rather than exact matched tests.
entries.condition: Different modalities, correction procedures, and recording setups limit direct equivalence.
entries.quote: we therefore caution that the phoneme decoding and speech synthesis comparisons made here should not be viewed as exact, matched performance tests but rather ballpark estimates.

entries.text: No language model or linguistic correction was used: the authors sought raw neural performance, and unit selection also omitted a concatenation cost/statistical prior.
entries.condition: Offline phoneme classification and offline Brain-to-Speech synthesis; no NLP, user-facing correction, or LM-assisted output.

entries.text: The authors state the dorsal hand/arm arrays are likely suboptimal and do not support fluent open-vocabulary communication; accuracy remains far below the near-100% performance aspired to for a speech BCI.
entries.condition: Two participants, two arrays each, dorsal precentral placement, fixed 420-word overt task.
entries.quote: we do not believe that these dorsal precentral gyrus signals from two Utah arrays are sufficient to support fluent open-vocabulary communication using a speech BCI

entries.text: LRR may leave acoustic contamination and may also remove genuine neural activity shared across electrodes, so its accuracy change does not isolate artifact contribution exactly.
entries.condition: T5 acoustic-decontamination analysis; within-block regression from the other electrodes.

entries.text: Classification was offline on prompted, labeled phoneme snippets; the authors say a clinical system must decode unlabeled continuous speech and free-running phoneme decoding remains future work.
entries.condition: Overt word production only; no attempted/silent speech decoder, continuous phoneme stream, or closed-loop speech BCI was evaluated.
entries.quote: free-running phoneme decoding from intracortical neural activity is a key next step for future work.

entries.text: The neural onset correction was limited to first phonemes because later-phoneme neural timing was unreliable; its correction effect is therefore unknown for later phonemes.
entries.condition: 18-class first-phoneme evaluation; later phonemes in multi-phoneme words were not realigned and evaluated.
entries.quote: It thus remains an open challenge to quantify and mitigate the effect of voice onset biases for the later phonemes of a word.

entries.text: The authors say auditory feedback may contribute to decoding, although pre-voice decoding and prior unvoiced-orofacial results suggest feedback effects are limited; the processes are not definitively disentangled.
entries.condition: Overt speech and motor-cortical recordings; no attempted-speech condition to separate articulation from feedback.

entries.text: Figure 6 showcases selected intelligible/borderline examples, but a separate random set showed most synthesis trials were not intelligible.
entries.condition: T5 offline synthesis; selected showcase versus randomly chosen examples; not a listener intelligibility test.
entries.quote: Supplementary Audio 2 presents another 47 randomly chosen example words which demonstrate that most synthesis trials were not intelligible.

entries.text: Participants received no online feedback that could let them adapt their neural activity; the authors frame offline performance as a lower bound.
entries.condition: Offline decoding/synthesis; no closed-loop use-time behavior or user adaptation measured.

entries.text: Unit selection compared each test neural feature with training features using cosine similarity, selected 150 ms audio snippets at 10 ms steps, and did not use a concatenation cost.
entries.unit: ms snippet; ms step; ms overlap
entries.condition: T5 speech synthesis; training library excludes test-fold words; no linguistic/statistical sequence prior.

entries.text: For synthesis, each 650 ms neural window was represented by thirteen 50 ms bins; PCA retained at least 70% variance (25 components here), with clipping, z-score and PCA statistics fit on training folds only.
entries.condition: T5 synthesis; 10-fold CV; test words absent from training folds.

entries.text: Logistic-regression figures used different CV schemes: leave-one-out for Figs. 3A/F and 5D, 20-fold for Figs. 4 and 5E/F, and 10 repetitions of 10-fold CV for Fig. 3 sweeps.
entries.condition: Within-participant utterance classification; T5/T11 separate; reported test outputs are offline.

entries.text: No random seeds are reported for CV partitioning, RNN initialization/augmentation, or random electrode subsampling; the RNN is described as one 10-fold evaluation, not repeated independent training runs.
entries.condition: CV repetitions are reported for logistic hyperparameter sweeps, but seed values and independent run variance are not reported.
entries.quote: The RNN was trained and evaluated across 10 folds of the data, such that each spoken phoneme utterance appeared in the test set once.

entries.text: The paper does not report a held-out-speaker test or cross-participant transfer; folds are formed from each participant’s utterances, so speaker-generalization performance is unknown.
entries.condition: Two participants, T5 and T11; results are participant-specific; no leave-one-speaker-out evaluation.

entries.text: For phoneme classification the paper does not say whether repeated instances of a prompted word were grouped into a single fold; vocabulary overlap across train/test folds is therefore unspecified.
entries.condition: Utterance-level CV is described; the fixed prompt vocabulary contains 420 words, with repeated presentations per participant.

entries.text: A dedicated validation/selection set is not described for the manually tuned LRR hyperparameters; the data used for that manual tuning are not specified.
entries.condition: LRR alpha=400 and eta0=0.0000004; regression fit separately within each block using voicing-epoch samples.

entries.text: RNN-specific input normalization is not fully specified: earlier HLFP clipping/smoothing is described, but no RNN-specific z-score or feature scaling procedure is stated.
entries.condition: RNN input uses 192 HLFP channels over 50 bins; unlike logistic regression, methods do not describe fold-wise z-scoring/PCA for RNN inputs.

entries.text: No use-time confirmation, rejection, or user correction interaction is reported; the study evaluates offline decoder outputs rather than a communication interface.
entries.condition: No online feedback or closed-loop interaction; prompted overt speech data only.

entries.text: The paper does not report confidence intervals or independent-run variability for the headline classification accuracies; variability shown for sweeps is standard deviation across 10 CV repetitions.
entries.condition: Headline scores are single cross-validated estimates; Fig. 3 sweep shading is SD, not uncertainty intervals for all headline scores.
entries.quote: Shading denotes standard deviation across 10 repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation.

entries.text: The 420-word dictionary and long analysis windows can let the classifier exploit adjacent-phoneme context; long windows can also delay output in a closed-loop BCI.
entries.unit: words; ms window with peak performance
entries.condition: Offline, audio-aligned phoneme classification; open-vocabulary implications are not directly tested.

entries.text: Acoustic-contamination screening included human ECoG and intracortical recordings and a rat micro-ECoG recording.
entries.condition: Human speech production and perception; rat sound perception; electrophysiological recordings

entries.text: The study assessed 20 datasets from 5 research centers.
entries.condition: Speech production and sound perception contamination assessment
entries.quote: Assessment of the presence or absence of contamination for 20 datasets from 5 different research centers.

entries.text: They measured Pearson correlations between neural and audio power across all frequency-bin pairs to form an audio-neural correlation matrix.
entries.condition: Each recording channel; neural and audio spectrograms

entries.text: The statistical criterion compares diagonal contamination-matrix values with values from shuffled matrices.
entries.condition: Contamination-specific same-frequency correlation assessment

entries.text: Roussel et al. compared ECoG decoders with and without 90-200 Hz features in two contaminated participants: an important increase for P2, a limited one for P5.
entries.condition: ECoG decoding of acoustic speech features; participants P2 and P5
entries.quote: from 90 to 200 Hz resulted in an important increase in decoding performance for P2 and only a limited improvement of decoding accuracy for participant P5.
entries.loc: 3.2 Potential influence of contamination on speech decoding

entries.text: They recommend assessing and eliminating acoustic contamination before studying cortical speech dynamics.
entries.condition: Speech-related electrophysiological recordings

entries.text: The study classified the full General American phoneme inventory with ECoG from 4 subjects.
entries.condition: General American English phoneme production; ECoG
entries.quote: In this study, we investigated words that span the entire set of phonemes in the General American accent using ECoG with 4 subjects.

entries.text: Phoneme onsets were manually labeled from visual and auditory changes in microphone audio; features used 150-ms windows stepped by 50 ms from 300 ms before to 300 ms after onset.
entries.condition: ECoG features aligned to within-word phoneme onset

entries.text: Phonemes were classified with linear discriminant analysis (LDA) using the 140 features with the lowest p-values.
entries.condition: ECoG phoneme classification; selected features from training data

entries.text: Subject NU2 had the best consonant performance, correctly classifying 36.1% of consonant phonemes.
entries.condition: Consonant phoneme classification; subject NU2; ECoG
entries.quote: Subject NU2 had the highest overall performance, in which 36.1% of consonant phonemes were correctly classified.

entries.text: Vowel accuracy averaged 19.2±3.7% across subjects versus 12.9% chance, with NU2 best at 23.9%.
entries.condition: Vowel phoneme classification; all subjects; best subject NU2; ECoG
entries.quote: Average classification performance for vowels across all subjects was 19.2±3.7%, also significantly greater than chance (12.9%, p<0.01, t-test), with the best performance in NU2 of 23.9%.

entries.text: Overall phoneme accuracy averaged 20.4±9.8% across subjects versus 7.4% chance.
entries.condition: All phonemes; averaged across subjects; ECoG

entries.text: T5 and T8 had two arrays each, with 96 electrodes per array, in dorsal motor-cortex hand knob.
entries.condition: Participants T5 and T8; left motor cortex; speech production

entries.condition: Single-trial syllable decoding; participants T5 and T8; cross-validated

entries.quote: Word decoding accuracies were 83.5% for T5 (11 classes, chance was 9.1%) and 61.5% for T8 (11 classes, chance was 9.3%).

entries.text: The authors tested a large condition-invariant signal (CIS) as a population-level movement-initiation motif.
entries.condition: Speaking-related neural population dynamics
entries.quote: The first population dynamics motif we tested for was a specific form of population-level structure at the initiation of movement: a large condition-invariant signal, previously described in Kaufman et al. (2016) .

entries.text: The text reports microphone recordings of prompts and voice, but does not state that neural onset markers or acoustic/microphonic contamination were assessed.
entries.condition: Speech task audio and intracortical neural recordings

entries.text: High-gamma cortical surface electrical potentials (CSEPs) were recorded from 4 human subjects.
entries.condition: Left-hemisphere ECoG during spoken speech production
entries.quote: Briefly, four native English speaking human subjects underwent chronic implantation of a subdural electrocortigraphic (ECoG) array over the left hemisphere as part of their clinical treatment of epilepsy.

entries.text: The task covered 57 potential CV syllables formed from 19 consonants and 3 vowels.
entries.condition: Read-aloud consonant-vowel syllables; ECoG
entries.quote: The subjects read aloud consonant-vowel (CV) syllables composed of 19 consonants followed by one of three vowels (/a/, /i/ or /u/), for a total of 57 potential consonant-vowel syllables.

entries.text: For Subject 1's CV task, the Results sentence reports 55.1 ± 2.3% for logistic regression and 44.6 ± 3.2% for deep networks, both against 1.8% chance, despite calling this the highest deep-network result.

entries.text: For Subject 1's consonant task, the Results sentence reports 59.0 ± 2.2% for logistic regression and 51.2 ± 1.8% for deep networks, both against 5.3% chance.

entries.text: PCD was applied to intracranial recordings from 54 patients undergoing intraoperative speech tasks during DBS implantation.
entries.condition: Intracranial recordings; intraoperative speech task; DBS implantation

entries.loc: Results: PCD performance in acoustic contaminated iEEG data

entries.text: The described subcortical DBS mapping recordings included microelectrode recordings and LFPs from a macro ring 3 mm above the microelectrode tip.
entries.condition: Intraoperative subcortical mapping; STN or GPi DBS

entries.text: The phase-coupling decomposition (PCD) denoiser was compared with common average reference (CAR) and independent component analysis (ICA).

entries.text: A densely connected convolutional neural network (DenseNet) classified consonants from ECoG signals.
entries.condition: Consonant decoding; ECoG; reserved testing data

entries.text: The decoder comparison covered Subject A, where CAR and ICA gains exceeded PCD gain; Subject B, where PCD outperformed CAR and ICA; and Subject C, with no artifact.

entries.quote: We tested the decoding method in three different cases: (i) CAR and ICA gain is greater than PCD gain (Subject A), (ii) PCD outperforms CAR and ICA (Subject B), and (iii) data have no artifact (Subject C).

entries.quote: Figure 7bshows that consonant classification accuracy is similar or better when PCD is applied as compared with classification on raw data.

entries.text: The authors credit their own earlier work: dorsal hand-knob signals already discriminated a small number of syllables and words.
entries.quote: These signals could be used to discriminate between a small number of syllables and words with high accuracy.

entries.text: The authors credit Roussel and colleagues for raising the microphonic-contamination confound.
entries.quote: The second confound, which was recently raised by Roussel and colleagues, is that mechanical vibrations due to speaking might cause microphonic artifacts in the neural recordings.

Accuracy was much higher in T5 than in T11.

entries.text: Discussion reports the RNN at 33.9% against 29.6% logistic regression.
entries.condition: T5, 39 phonemes
entries.quote: Leveraging a more computationally expressive machine learning approach for phoneme classification, we obtained a modest performance improvement using an RNN (33.9% accuracy, compared to 29.6% using logistic regression).

entries.quote: For this analysis we also restricted our trials to match the trial count of the participant with the highest performance in Mugler and colleagues and used an equivalent 600 millisecond window centered on voice onset (Supplementary Fig.

entries.text: Mugler et al. labelled each phoneme onset within each word by hand from the microphone signal.
entries.condition: ECoG, 4 subjects
entries.quote: We inspected visual and auditory spectral changes in the microphone signal to manually label the onset of each phoneme within each word.

entries.text: ICA always gave the lowest consonant decoding accuracy in the three cases.
entries.condition: DenseNet consonant decoding, Subjects A-C
entries.quote: Here, it is interesting to mention that in the three evaluated cases, regardless of the electrode gain performance, ICA always resulted in the lowest consonant decoding accuracy, suggesting that relevant neural activity that encodes speech has also been removed during the ICA denoising.

entries.text: The onset-realignment test used T5's first phonemes only.
entries.condition: T5
entries.quote: To measure the impact of this confound, we trained separate decoders to classify the first phoneme of T5’s spoken words using 1) the original neural data windows, which were aligned to voice onset as in Fig.

entries.text: Logistic regression used leave-one-out cross-validation over phoneme instances.
entries.quote: The logistic regression model was trained using the Scikit-learn library in a leave-one-out cross-validation setup using default parameters except for the “lbfgs” optimization setting and L2 regularization value (λ = 100) to suppress overfitting.

entries.text: The authors concede that with a 420-word dictionary longer windows may exploit adjacent phonemes.
entries.quote: First, given the limited dictionary size in this study (420 words), increasing the decoding window may allow the classifier to exploit neural correlates of adjacent phonemes in a way that is not representative of what could be expected during open vocabulary decoding.

entries.text: Methods: 256 of Mugler's 320 words present; the remaining 64 filled with similar words.
entries.quote: To fill out the remaining 64 words, we picked similar words from the 190 additional words in our overall dataset.

entries.text: Phoneme onsets were identified from audio.
entries.quote: Phoneme onsets were identified from audio recordings, and their identities were then classified from neural features consisting of each electrode’s binned action potential counts or high-frequency local field potential power.

entries.text: The authors frame LRR as a novel use of a stimulation-artifact decontamination procedure.
entries.quote: To account for this contamination, we implemented two different approaches: 1) classification of each word’s first phoneme using pre-voice onset activity, and 2) the novel use of a decontamination procedure previously deployed for electrical stimulation artifact reduction.

entries.text: The authors frame both confounds as having received little prior attention.
entries.quote: Here we investigated two potential limitations which have received little prior attention.

entries.text: LRR can also remove genuine shared neural signal.
entries.quote: However, we note that the LRR technique does not guarantee that all acoustic contamination is eliminated (which would cause us to under-estimate the contribution of microphonic pickup to decoding accuracy), and it also can subtract out genuine neural signal that is shared across electrodes (which would cause us to over-estimate the contribution).

entries.text: The centred 500-ms window gave 54.9% on first phonemes, the comparison point for the pre-voice window.
entries.quote: For comparison, using a 500 ms neural window centered on the phoneme’s voice onset (which we expect to better capture phoneme production-specific neural activity, in addition to potential acoustic contamination and auditory feedback) yielded an accuracy of 54.9% (Fig. 4D).

entries.text: Anumanchipalli et al. tested their decoder on silently mimed speech to rule out reliance on auditory feedback.
entries.quote: To rule out the possibility that the decoder is relying on the auditory feedback of participants’ vocalization, and to simulate a setting where subjects do not overtly vocalize, we tested our decoder on silently mimed speech.

questions.q: Do these results establish attempted-speech, continuous, or online speech-BCI performance?
questions.answer: No. The decoders were evaluated offline on visually prompted overt speech with phoneme labels; attempted-speech and free-running online decoding were not evaluated.

questions.q: How much can the headline decoding scores be attributed to overt-speech confounds?
questions.answer: The authors report a modest effect: neural realignment lowers first-phoneme accuracy, and LRR lowers full-class accuracy, but neither analysis exactly isolates or eliminates the artifact contribution.

questions.q: Does the evaluation demonstrate cross-speaker generalization?
questions.answer: No held-out-speaker or cross-participant transfer test is reported; the folds are participant-specific.

questions.q: How intelligible is the synthesized speech?
questions.answer: Overall spectral correlation was above the random-unit chance estimate, but the paper says most randomly chosen synthesis trials were not intelligible; selected figure examples are not representative of all trials.

questions.q: Were language models, user confirmation, or online correction used?
questions.answer: No. The paper reports raw neural performance without an LM or concatenation prior, and it does not describe a use-time confirmation/correction interface.

questions.q: Is public code available for checking omitted training or evaluation conditions?
questions.answer: No public code repository is linked by the paper; the acknowledgement only refers to RNN code documentation.
